conditions.B: close old page, open cached new page

scope: HTTP-cache cold/reload/cached-new-page diagnosis on the original 856/d360 runtime and Chromium151; native observation, no runtime optimization or physical-device performance claim
interpretation: The HTTP reload excess lies in native renderer NavigationClient handling and overlapping GPU command-buffer destruction, with low thread CPU in these long events. Cached new pages move much of the lifecycle cost to page creation. This diagnoses the observed browser teardown wait; it is not cache-transfer work or a measured runtime speedup.
limits: Trace intervals describe recorded wall time; thread CPU is native whole-event tdur, not an invented utilization estimate. Nested named events overlap and are not added as total CPU.

Original build and browser are matched, but host resources and tracing overhead differ from the historical official run. One source test and then emitted tests overlapped the first order; later samples ran without these processes. See environment receipt.
This experiment covers HTTP warm. Independent controlled SW traces are in startup-sw.json; persistent browser-restart still has historical success receipts and no new native trace.
No physical GPU/iOS/Android, deployment/TLS or generic browser performance claim. No runtime code, original 180-second readiness gate or cache response substitution was changed.

Native renderer/GPU intervals and temporal ordering localize the wait, but this trace does not contain a uniquely joined renderer-to-GPU synchronous IPC reply flow or native call stack. It is not an intervention proving that GPU destruction alone causes every part of the wait.
